reviewers.interpretation_notes: Per the brief, I evaluated both the strongest form (the instruments contain explicit travel restrictions, permits, penalties, or movement monitoring) and the weakest defensible form (the instruments create a mechanism that could enable such restrictions without further council action). I read the full consolidated District Policy text (Charter Bylaw 24000, office consolidation April 2026, 50 pages) as the primary evidence, plus the adopting council report. I did not read all 15 individual District Plan bylaws line by line; per the policy's own Chapter 1, those plans consist of maps showing where the District Policy applies plus area-specific land-use policies.

I treated indirect changes to street design, parking, transportation investment, or development patterns as effects on travel conditions, not restrictions on where a person may go. A mechanism required an operative authorization tied to crossing district boundaries or monitoring individual movement. The possibility that Council could enact a different bylaw in the future was not treated as a current mechanism.

round2_positions.interpretation_notes: Position unchanged from round 1 and now shared by all three reviewers; this is convergence on the primary text, not toward a majority. Per the brief I evaluated both the strongest form (explicit travel restrictions, permits, penalties, or movement monitoring in the adopted instruments) and the weakest defensible form (a mechanism that could enable such restrictions without further council action). For round 2 I re-fetched the April 2026 office consolidation and City Plan Bylaw 20000 on 2026-09-01 and verified every quote I rely on, including those adopted from Reviewer A. I treated policies that change travel conditions (parking pricing, road design, mode-shift targets, infrastructure financing) as effects on convenience and cost, not restrictions on where a person may go; that boundary matches Reviewer A's and I state it explicitly because it is where the honest steelman lives.

I evaluated both explicit restrictions and mechanisms that could theoretically enable them. I differentiate between land-use/infrastructure policies that influence travel choices and instruments that regulate or restrict individual movement. I have replaced my unverified URL from Round 1 with the verified primary legal and policy documents surfaced by the other reviewers.

My verdict remains unchanged after cross-review. I distinguish policies that affect urban form, parking prices, street design, or the relative convenience of travel modes from provisions that control where an individual may go. The documents contain behaviour-shaping planning tools, but no operative authority tied to crossing district boundaries, obtaining travel permission, penalizing inter-district trips, or monitoring identifiable residents for that purpose. The freedom-of-movement clause is not an immutable constitutional guarantee, and Council can amend planning documents. Amendability is not a present restriction mechanism.
